q: Sound is a form of ____ that is transferred from one place to another in a certain medium.
e: Sound is mechanical energy transmitted through a medium via particle vibrations.

q: Sound wave is produced by a ____ placed in a medium.
e: The initial disturbance that creates a sound wave is always a vibrating source.

q: The pressure changes occur ____ in the medium by vibrating object.
e: Sound propagation involves alternating regions of high pressure (compression) and low pressure (rarefaction).

q: Sound wave propagates as a series of ____ like longitudinal waves on a vibrating spring.
e: These alternating pressure regions are the mechanism by which longitudinal sound waves travel.

q: Unlike electromagnetic waves, sound waves need a ____ to propagate.
e: Sound is a mechanical wave and cannot exist or travel without material particles to transmit the vibration.

q: Sound wave cannot travel through ____.
e: The absence of particles in a vacuum prevents the transmission of sound energy.

q: The compression is created in the medium as the vibrating object ____.
e: Forward motion of the vibrating source forces adjacent particles closer, increasing local pressure.

q: The compression region has ____.
e: Compression is defined by an increase in molecular density and pressure within the medium.

q: When the object moves back, the molecules are spread out and ____ is created and the pressure of that region is low.
e: Rarefaction is the region of low pressure and density that follows a compression in a sound wave.

q: The average person can only hear sound that has a frequency higher than ____ and lower than $20\,000 \text{ Hz}$.
e: The lower limit of the human audible range is typically 20 hertz.

q: This interval of frequency is called the ____ (or) hearing range.
e: The audible range defines the spectrum of sound frequencies detectable by the human ear.

q: Sound waves with frequencies greater than $20\,000 \text{ Hz}$ are called ____.
e: Ultrasound refers to sound frequencies that are too high for human hearing.

q: Some objects vibrating with frequencies under $20 \text{ Hz}$ produces sound which cannot be heard by ____.
e: Frequencies below the human hearing threshold are inaudible to people but may be detected by other animals.

q: This is called ____.
e: Infrasound refers to sound waves with frequencies below 20 Hz.

q: Generally, the speed of sound depends on the ____ of the medium.
e: The physical properties of the medium, particularly its density and elasticity, determine how fast sound travels.

q: The denser the medium is, the ____ the speed because the particles of the medium are tightly bound together.
e: In denser media, particles are closer together, allowing the vibrational disturbance to be transferred more rapidly.

q: At $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ the speed of sound in air is ____.
e: This is the standard reference speed of sound in air at freezing temperature.

q: Whenever the air temperature increases by $1^{\circ}\text{C}$, speed of sound will increase by ____.
e: Sound travels faster in warmer air because the molecules have more kinetic energy to transmit the wave.

q: The speed of sound in air can be expressed as ____.
e: This formula calculates the speed of sound in air based on the absolute temperature $T$ in Kelvin.

q: Here $T$ is given in ____ and $v$ in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
e: The temperature variable in the exact speed of sound formula must be in absolute Kelvin.

q: The above relation can be approximated by ____.
e: This linear approximation is often used for quick calculations of sound speed at different Celsius temperatures.

q: In air medium, the speed of sound increases by ____ with temperature rise by one degree ($1^{\circ}\text{C}$ or $1\text{K}$).
e: For every degree Celsius increase in temperature, the speed of sound in air increases by approximately 0.6 metres per second.
